nature-nbs-034.title: Blue carbon: the climate value of coastal mud
nature-nbs-034.text: Coastal mud can hold carbon for millennia. Blue carbon is carbon taken up and stored by living marine systems, especially coastal ones, in ways people can manage. Most often it means the carbon captured by tidal marshes, mangroves and seagrass meadows. These vegetated coastal ecosystems bury carbon fast, piling it up in their soils and sediments. Those sediments lack oxygen, so the carbon can be preserved for decades to millennia, far longer than most carbon stocks on land. The term was coined in 2009 to stress that these ecosystems store far more than their share of the world's carbon. Seagrass, salt marshes and mangroves are sometimes called 'blue forests', in contrast to green forests on land. The flip side is stark. When these ecosystems are damaged or lost, they release their carbon back to the air. Managing them counts as an ocean-based, biological form of {{ref:nature-clim-138}}, and it can serve both climate mitigation and ecosystem-based adaptation. How effective blue carbon is over the long term, though, is still debated.

nature-nbs-064.title: Coastal erosion: the sea takes back the land
nature-nbs-064.text: In 1917 the village of Hallsands in Devon was washed into the sea. Shingle had been dredged from its bay, leaving it unprotected. Coastal erosion is the loss of land, or long-term removal of sediment and rock, along a coastline. Waves, currents, tides, wind-driven water, ice and storms all do the work. They act through the hydraulic force of water, abrasion by hurled stones, attrition as stones grind each other down, and seawater chemically dissolving rock. Softer rock erodes faster than harder rock, carving tunnels, arches and pillars, until over time the coast evens out. Storms can erode coasts hundreds of times faster than normal weather. Rising seas let waves reach further inland, speeding the retreat. The losses compound. Erosion destroys the dunes, wetlands, beaches and barrier islands that buffer storms, and it reduces biodiversity. It damages infrastructure and property, raises protection costs, and harms tourism and fisheries.

nature-nbs-053.title: Coastal management: defending where people crowd
nature-nbs-053.text: Coastal zones cover less than 15% of Earth's land, yet host more than 40% of the world's people. Nearly 1.2 billion people live within 100 km of a coastline and 100 m of sea level. Coastal management is the work of defending coasts against flooding and erosion, including techniques that stop erosion to claim land. Its importance is growing as climate change speeds up the rise of the seas this century. Before the 1950s, the norm was hard structures such as {{ref:nature-nbs-071}}, sloping stone revetments and sand-trapping walls. From the late 1940s, cost and ugliness pushed engineers toward artificial beaches and stabilized dunes that copy natural protection. One lesson came hard. Measures often worked locally but made problems worse elsewhere, sometimes tens of kilometres away.

nature-nbs-040.title: Managed retreat: moving out of harm's way
nature-nbs-040.text: Kiribati, a low-lying country facing flooding, is planning to relocate its people. Managed retreat is the planned, coordinated movement of people, buildings and infrastructure away from places at risk. It can answer floods, wildfire, drought and other hazards, and its form depends on the place, the hazard and local policy. Retreating from high-risk areas such as floodplains reduces exposure. Rising seas are now drawing the attention of politicians, insurers and residents of low-lying coasts. Retreat is controversial. Programs have met lawsuits and resistance from residents worried about home values and insurance costs. Yet more communities consider it as the costs of adaptation rise. One New Zealand coastal hazards expert argues retreat is mainly a social and political issue, not a technical one. Whether migration counts as adaptation is itself debated; the IPCC says it may or may not.

nature-nbs-071.title: Seawalls: holding the line in concrete
nature-nbs-071.text: At least 43 percent of Japan's coastline is lined with seawalls or similar structures. Yet in 2011 the tsunami overwhelmed seawalls in most areas. A seawall is a hard coastal defense built where the sea acts directly on the land, to protect people, property and activities from tides, waves or tsunamis. It works by reflecting wave energy back out to sea. That reflected energy has costs. It can scour and lower the beach in front, and the wall can speed erosion of neighboring unprotected coasts. Being fixed, a seawall clashes with a moving coast and blocks the exchange of sediment between land and sea. Rising seas raise both normal water levels and storm waves, which existing walls may not withstand. High costs and side effects have led to more use of soft options such as beach replenishment. A cost-benefit approach helps decide whether a wall is worth it.

nature-nbs-069.title: Oyster reefs: living breakwaters that filter the sea
nature-nbs-069.text: Over two centuries, 85% of the world's oyster reefs have been removed. An oyster reef is a dense colony of oysters that builds up into a large reef, also called an oyster bed, bank or bar. New reefs start on stone or hard debris, because oyster larvae must settle on hard surfaces. Young oysters then settle on older shells, and the reef grows. Overharvesting, lime production and coastal degradation drove the decline. What was lost was valuable. Oysters filter phytoplankton and organic matter from the water, buffering estuaries against eutrophication. Reefs trap sediment and damp waves, and are recognized as green infrastructure for shoreline protection. Their nooks shelter prey and young animals. Restored intertidal eastern oyster reefs can match natural oyster densities and regain stability in about 6 years.

nature-nbs-063.title: Beach nourishment: buying time with sand
nature-nbs-063.text: The first US beach nourishment project was at Coney Island, New York, in 1922–1923. Since 1923 the US has spent $9 billion rebuilding beaches. Beach nourishment replaces sand lost through erosion or longshore drift, the movement of sand along a shore, with sediment brought from elsewhere. A wider beach soaks up wave energy across the surf zone, shielding buildings behind it from storm surges and unusually high tides. It counts as {{ref:nature-nbs-073}}, keeping the beach and avoiding the harms of hard structures. But it must be repeated, because it eases erosion without removing its causes. The new sand's grain size must closely match the native sand. It can also bury seafloor creatures and cut light to nearby reefs and seagrass. Benefits include higher property values and more tourism, though high erosion rates can make it financially impractical.

nature-nbs-054.title: Five ways to answer a moving coast
nature-nbs-054.text: Faced with a changing coast, people have five broad choices. They can abandon the land. They can retreat or realign, moving back in a planned way. They can armor the shore with hard structures. They can build defenses out to sea. Or they can raise land and buildings. The right choice depends on local sea-level change, landforms, sediment supply and erosion. Social, economic and political factors weigh just as much. Building seaward can create valuable new land, but it leaves developed coasts exposed to {{ref:nature-nbs-066}}, which traps habitats against fixed defenses. Where land has little economic value, limited intervention is an option. It lets salt marshes and dunes develop and absorb wave energy. {{ref:nature-gov-123}} offers another route, keeping development out of erosion- or flood-prone areas in the first place.

nature-nbs-073.title: Soft engineering: shores held by plants and logs
nature-nbs-073.text: Around the Detroit River, 38 soft engineering projects cost $17.3 million and showed strong economic and social benefits. Soft engineering is a shoreline management practice that uses ecological principles and natural materials to stabilize shores and protect waterside habitats. It places plants, stones, sand, logs and similar materials to reduce erosion, soften the edge between land and water and lower restoration costs. Its principles are to imitate nature, use gentle slopes that spread wave energy, use living 'soft armor' and mix materials for biodiversity. The most basic technique is planting native vegetation whose roots bind the soil. Other tools include coir logs of coconut fibre, live stakes and fascines, brush mattresses, live cribwalls and vegetated riprap. Coastal engineering shifted toward the natural environment late in the 20th century. Soft and hard methods can be blended, especially on fast-flowing waters.

nature-nbs-041.title: Managed realignment: letting the sea back in
nature-nbs-041.text: At Abbott's Hall Farm in Essex, five breaches were cut in an old sea wall. The sea flowed in and created nearly 280 hectares of salt marsh. That is managed realignment: deliberately removing or breaching coastal flood defenses so the sea can reclaim land and form natural soft landforms. In the UK its main aim is coastal stability, swapping hard defenses for salt marsh and similar features. The obvious drawback is that land is given up to the sea. But the new marsh buffers land further inland by absorbing water and damping waves. Realignment also replaces intertidal habitat lost to erosion and to {{ref:nature-nbs-066}}. Results have been very unpredictable, because few sites are monitored consistently.

nature-nbs-060.title: Sand dune stabilization: holding the coast's sand bank
nature-nbs-060.text: In about 30 years, nearly 75% of the Mediterranean's coastal dunes were damaged or destroyed, mainly by tourism. Sand dune stabilization is the coastal management practice of keeping dunes from eroding. Dunes protect inland areas from storms, waves and seawater, and can resupply eroded beaches with sand. They also shelter specialized plants and animals, including rare and endangered species. Vegetation binds the sand. Without it, wind carries sand inland in a process called sand encroachment. Stabilizing a dune combines planting against wind and water, wooden sand fences that hold sand, and footpaths that keep walkers off. Unlike hard defenses, whose end effects erode neighboring coasts, dune work counts as a soft technique. Without public understanding and support, it is virtually impossible.

nature-nbs-051.title: Oyster reef restoration: rebuilding a lost reef
nature-nbs-051.text: By 2011, an estimated 85% of the world's oyster reefs had been lost to over-harvesting, destructive fishing, pollution and disease. Oyster reef restoration is the work of repairing and rebuilding them. Projects aim for a working three-dimensional reef that supports biodiversity, protects shorelines, traps sediment and cleans water. Sites are chosen by surveying salinity, water quality, past reefs, the seabed, disease, predators and more. The payoff can be real. Restored reefs can recover oyster densities that match healthy natural reefs. Cleaner water benefits commercial and recreational fishing, boating and ecotourism, and projects create and safeguard jobs. One caution: introducing non-native oyster species can do more harm than good.

nature-nbs-038.title: Deep blue carbon: the ocean's largest, least manageable store
nature-nbs-038.text: Most ocean carbon lies far from any coast. Deep blue carbon is carbon stored in deep ocean waters and the sea floor of the high seas, beyond national jurisdictions. It covers continental shelf waters, deep-sea waters and the sea floor beneath them, and makes up 90% of all ocean carbon. It is seen as harder to manage, because data on how permanent these stores are is lacking. Below about 3 km, CO2 becomes liquid and sinks, because it is denser than the seawater around it. Techniques being explored include seaweed farming, ocean fertilization, artificial upwelling and basalt storage.

nature-nbs-037.title: Seagrass meadows: a sliver of seafloor, a big carbon sink
nature-nbs-037.text: Seagrass covers only 0.1% of the ocean floor, yet it accounts for roughly 10–18% of total oceanic carbon burial. Meadows bury that carbon in their sediments. Worldwide they may store as much as 19.9 Pg of organic carbon, where one Pg is a billion tonnes. Burial rates vary with species, sediment and depth, averaging about 138 g C m−2 yr−1.

nature-nbs-039.title: Does seaweed count as blue carbon?
nature-nbs-039.text: Whether seaweed forests count as blue carbon ecosystems is contentious. They are strong candidates, because macroalgae are highly productive and line coasts worldwide. A 2016 report estimated they could sequester 173 TgC per year, with a range of 61–268, but the estimate is very uncertain. Their carbon can be buried in nearby sediments, exported to the deep ocean, or released as dissolved carbon that resists breakdown. Tracking where it ends up is very hard. Until long-term storage is proven, precise estimates of their capacity are lacking.

nature-nbs-035.title: Tidal marshes: carbon stored in roots and mud
nature-nbs-035.text: Tidal marsh deposits can be up to 8 m deep. Tidal marshes are intertidal ecosystems of non-woody plants, and they are important carbon sinks. Sediment builds up fast and decay happens largely without oxygen, so carbon stays locked in roots and buried plant matter. Much of their growth is underground. Salt marshes cover roughly 22,000 to 400,000 km2 worldwide and bury an estimated 210 g C m−2 yr−1. They also shelter birds and young fish, protect coasts from storm surge and flooding, and cut the nutrients reaching coastal waters.

nature-nbs-047.title: Coral reef restoration: replanting the reef
nature-nbs-047.text: Half the world's coral has disappeared since 1970. Coral reef restoration covers the natural and human-led processes that restore damaged reefs. The stakes are high: reefs host over 25% of marine life, buffer coasts from storms and erosion, and support food, jobs and tourism. Restoration has grown in prominence because of unprecedented die-offs around the planet. The usual method is to break mature corals into fragments, grow them on lines or supports, and transplant them once large enough. This gardening may not save every species. Instead, it can help natural recovery and widen a species' gene pool. One worry is that some propagated corals may spread like invasive species and harm biodiversity.

nature-nbs-058.title: Shoreline mapping: tracking a line that never stays put
nature-nbs-058.text: Where exactly is the shoreline? The question is hard, because coasts are dynamic and tides shift the line at any moment. Shoreline mapping records where the shore is and how it moves over time, a basic need for coastal scientists, engineers and managers. Data come from historical maps, aerial photographs used since the 1920s, beach surveys, remote sensing and video. Monitoring shows how the shore has moved and supports predictions of future change.

nature-nbs-042.title: Buyout programs: when government buys the house
nature-nbs-042.text: Valmeyer, Illinois, and Isle de Jean Charles, Louisiana, moved as whole communities. In buyout programs, government buys at-risk properties and relocates or demolishes them, a form of managed retreat. Relocation has been used inland and on coasts after severe flooding and hurricanes. Sometimes single homes are bought after a disaster.

nature-nbs-072.title: Natural coastal barriers: living seawalls
nature-nbs-072.text: After the tsunami of 26 December 2004, a UNEP report found less damage where mangroves, coral reefs or coastal vegetation were present. Natural coastal barriers are such ecosystems, which blunt tsunamis and storm surges like a living seawall. Reefs can damp waves as well as or better than artificial breakwaters. India took the lesson quickly. Weeks after the disaster, it began planting Casuarina and coconut saplings along its coast as a natural barrier.

nature-nbs-044.title: Mangroves are vanishing faster than rainforests
nature-nbs-044.text: Mangroves are being lost faster than inland tropical rainforests. At least 35% of global mangrove area is already gone, and the decline continues at 1-2% per year. Clearing for development, aquaculture and farming drives it, along with climate change. The climate cost is outsized. Mangroves make up only 0.7% of tropical forest area, yet their clearing contributes 10% of global CO2 emissions from deforestation. Rising seas add a test: a mangrove forest survives only if its sediment builds up as fast as the sea rises.

nature-eco-415.title: Mangrove restoration: why planting is not enough
nature-eco-415.text: Mangroves store three to four times more carbon than other tropical forests. Mangrove restoration rehabilitates degraded or destroyed mangrove forests so they return to something like their condition before disturbance. They are worth it. Mangroves filter water, nurture young fish, supply medicines, food and timber, and protect coasts from erosion and storm surges. The obvious approach often fails. Planting single-species stands in places thought suitable usually fails, because the trees' soil and water needs are not met. Better methods let damaged areas regrow naturally through {{ref:nature-eco-386}}, provided tidal and freshwater flows work and seedlings are available. Mangroves are among the easiest coastal systems to restore, because seedlings can survive where no adult trees remain. Success would need an estimated US$0.3–1.6 billion a year until 2050, and debt-for-nature swaps have been proposed to help pay. Long-term success depends on local communities taking part.

nature-nbs-046.title: REDD+ and mangroves: paying shrimp farmers to keep trees
nature-nbs-046.text: In Thailand, carbon markets pay farmers to keep mangroves standing. The money makes up for the income they forgo by not turning the forest into shrimp ponds, the opportunity cost of conservation. This applies REDD+, a UN mechanism that pays developing-country stakeholders to avoid deforestation, to protect and restore mangroves. The UN launched the REDD program in 2008 to cut emissions and strengthen forest carbon sinks.

nature-nbs-045.title: Bringing communities into mangrove restoration
nature-nbs-045.text: Mangrove projects without community support risk backlash and wasted money and effort. Stakeholder engagement means involving local people in planning, doing and maintaining restoration. Locals bring knowledge of their environment. Paid work and funding give them a reason to keep caring for the mangroves. Valuing the work is hard, though, because most mangrove services are indirect and never sold in markets.

nature-nbs-074.title: Hard engineering: concrete, steel and rock
nature-nbs-074.text: The Detroit River lost as much as 97% of its coastal wetlands to hard engineering. Hard engineering protects shorelines with non-living materials such as concrete, steel and rock to stop erosion and flooding. Its four main coastal structures are the seawall, revetment, {{ref:nature-nbs-056}} and breakwater. It mainly serves navigation, industry and commerce. The price has been steep. It destroyed biological communities, cut off waterside habitats and disrupted the natural movement of sediment. Every hard structure gives only temporary protection. Each also creates an end effect that erodes the neighboring coast.

nature-nbs-065.title: Soft, hard or leave: three answers to erosion
nature-nbs-065.text: Fifteen feet of marsh can absorb fifty percent of incoming wave energy. Coastal erosion has three common answers: soft controls, hard controls and relocation. Hard controls are more permanent: a seawall lasts about 50–100 years, and a sand-trapping {{ref:nature-nbs-056}} 30–40 years. Soft controls such as sandbags and beach nourishment slow erosion temporarily. Vegetated shores such as marshes ({{ref:nature-nbs-059}}) resist storms well. Relocation is the third option, though public support for retreat has typically been low.

nature-nbs-056.title: Groynes: walls that catch sand
nature-nbs-056.text: A groyne is a wall or barrier built at right angles to the coast. It traps sand carried along the shore and so builds up a beach. Sand piles up on one side, widening the beach, but beach material is lost on the other. Groynes are cheap, need little maintenance and are among the most common defenses, though many communities dislike their look. The last groyne in a series starves beaches further along of sand, a problem called terminal groyne syndrome.

nature-nbs-055.title: Hold the line: keeping the shore where it is
nature-nbs-055.text: Seawalls, groynes, detached breakwaters and revetments make up more than 70% of protected shorelines in Europe. They serve hold the line, a strategy that keeps the shoreline where it is, usually with permanent concrete and rock. Armoring often just moves the problem along the coast, and maintenance costs can eventually force a change of strategy. Holding the line need not mean concrete. Soft options such as beach nourishment and dune stabilization can do it by working with natural processes.

nature-nbs-059.title: Living shorelines: marsh in place of walls
nature-nbs-059.text: Bulkheads and seawalls can worsen erosion. A living shoreline protects shores and marshes using as many natural elements as possible instead of walls, and it buffers wave energy more effectively. It is a form of soft engineering. Common materials include sand, wetland plants, oyster reefs, underwater vegetation, stones and coir fibre logs. A typical design places a low rock sill or breakwater seeded with oyster spat, young oysters. The sill calms the water so marsh grasses can be planted behind it. The benefits are many: filtering runoff, creating habitat, absorbing waves and supporting fisheries, possibly at lower cost than seawalls. Projects move through site analysis, permits, preparation, installation, then maintenance and monitoring.

nature-nbs-068.title: Shrimp among the mangroves
nature-nbs-068.text: Expanding shrimp farms are a main cause of mangrove loss, even though the ponds depend on mangrove services. Integrated mangrove-shrimp aquaculture, or silvofishery, grows shrimp in ponds alongside planted mangroves. It relies on natural feed and wild shrimp brought in by the tides rather than chemicals and formulated feed, so running costs are low. Studies in Vietnam found profit peaks with 30%-50% mangrove cover, while rules requiring 60-80% cover have discouraged farmers. Benefits include biodiversity, blue carbon, coastal protection and steady income. Unequal sharing of timber income and conflicting policies hold it back.

nature-nbs-061.title: Dune plant zones: from salt spray to forest
nature-nbs-061.text: A beach dune has bands of plants. Foredune plants, facing the sea, must tolerate salt spray, strong winds and burial by blowing sand. On the dune plain and backdune, plants grow into dense 'dune mats' that hold the dune together. Once these non-woody plants are established, deeper-rooted shrubs can follow, and the shrub stage may give way to forest or chaparral. The wrong plant can backfire. In New Zealand, introduced marram grass built steep, storm-vulnerable dunes and crowded out native plants; it is now classed as a pest.

nature-nbs-052.title: Cultching: giving baby oysters somewhere to land
nature-nbs-052.text: Oyster larvae swim freely for about three weeks. Then they must attach to a hard surface to become spat, young oysters. Cultching lays down cultch, such as old shell, to give them that surface and rebuild a reef. Used oyster and clam shells from farmers and restaurants are cleaned and returned to the water. Pioneered for oyster farming in the early 19th century, cultching has been the most successful way to reform oyster beds.

nature-nbs-062.title: Climate-driven relocation: towns that move away
nature-nbs-062.text: Isle de Jean Charles in Louisiana, about 100 people, became the first total community migration in that state, driven by saltwater intrusion and rising seas. Climate-driven community relocation is the whole or partial abandonment of places, or plans to move their people, because of human-caused climate change. The causes often overlap: rising seas, flooding, land turning into wetland, coastal erosion, cyclones, droughts, water shortages and wildfires. Vunidogoloa became the first town in Fiji to be relocated, after persistent flooding, saltwater intrusion and erosion. In the Lake Chad Basin, 30,000,000 people are affected by droughts, floods and the lake's shrinking.

nature-nbs-049.title: Coral gardening: growing reefs in nurseries
nature-nbs-049.text: Most coral colonies grow only about an inch a year. Coral gardening speeds things up by growing small fragments in nurseries until mature, then moving them to damaged reefs. A wild colony is cut into pieces, which grow asexually into new colonies genetically identical to the parent. Fragmenting gives about an 8x increase in colony growth compared with the donor. Ocean nurseries hang fragments on lines or fix them to structures. Land nurseries grow them in tanks, shielded from storms, predators and disease.

nature-nbs-050.title: Microfragmentation: corals in months, not years
nature-nbs-050.text: In 2006 David Vaughan found a way to make reef-building corals grow much faster. Microfragmentation cuts live coral into very small pieces and fixes them to plugs in tanks. It relies on coral's ability to clone itself. Growth that took years now often takes months.

nature-nbs-066.title: Coastal squeeze: habitats trapped against the wall
nature-nbs-066.text: As seas rise, salt marsh naturally shifts inland. Coastal squeeze is what happens when it cannot: the habitat runs up against a seawall or other solid structure and is lost. Where walls block that retreat and sediment supply is limited, salt marsh cannot keep up with rising seas. Wetlands, salt marshes, mangroves and neighboring freshwater wetlands are especially vulnerable.

nature-nbs-067.title: Community-based mangrove management: locals as stewards
nature-nbs-067.text: When colonial and post-colonial states took control of mangroves, local people were alienated, and the forests were logged and farmed heavily. Community Based Mangrove Management reverses that. It shifts authority to local communities, with resource users directly involved, to conserve mangroves and support ways of making a living that can last. Community-managed mangroves show remarkable recovery, and local people have proved effective stewards. Success depends on communities' willingness to pay and on balancing ecological, economic and social goals.

nature-nbs-070.title: Sea rewilding: letting damaged seas heal
nature-nbs-070.text: More than 90% of the UK's historic seagrass meadows have been lost since the 1930s, and Europe's oyster stocks have fallen 95 per cent. Sea rewilding restores marine organisms and ecosystems so damaged seas can recover and thrive on their own. Methods include reintroducing or replenishing oysters, kelp and seagrass. It can capture carbon, support local economies through ecotourism and reverse biodiversity loss. Such projects are still less common at sea than on land.

openers.coastal-solutions: Where land meets sea, waves, currents, tides and storms carry sediment and rock away, and the shoreline retreats. People have long answered with hard defenses such as seawalls, but there are other choices: retreating, rebuilding beaches with sand, or stabilizing dunes. This chapter weighs them all, from managed retreat to deliberately breaching old sea defenses so salt marsh can return. It also meets the living defenders, oyster reefs and coastal plants, and the people who rebuild them. And it follows blue carbon, the carbon that coastal ecosystems take up and store in ways people can manage.

reviews.coastal-solutions: Coasts are eroding, seas are rising, and hard defenses such as seawalls and groynes protect one stretch while pushing the damage onto the next. Soft engineering offers another path: beach nourishment, dune planting, living shorelines, oyster reefs and restored mangroves that damp waves and still feed fish. Those same marshes, mangroves and seagrass meadows store blue carbon, so losing them releases it. Where defense costs too much, managed retreat, realignment and buyouts move people back, from Abbott's Hall Farm to Isle de Jean Charles. Throughout, success hinges on local communities, from shrimp farmers paid to keep mangroves to the stewards of community-managed forests.
